entries.description: 2B Remainder and factor theorem; Remainder theorem; Remainder Theorem. Division by x − a leaves remainder P(a). Proof uses P(x) = (x − a)Q(x) + R and substitution x = a.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone topic heading, theorem and proof are teaching reference evidence only.

entries.description: note to students: This allows you to skip the division algorithm when finding the remainder.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone teaching note is reference evidence only.

entries.description: example — Remainder of linear divisor. Find the remainder when P(x) = x⁹⁹ − 1 is divided by x + 1. Supplied solution: R = P(−1) = (−1)⁹⁹ − 1 = −2.
entries.exclusionReason: Worked example is reference evidence only.

entries.description: example — Finding polynomials with given remainder. P(x) = x³ + 3x² + ax + b has remainder 4 on division by x − 2 and remainder −8 on division by x + 1. Find a and b. Supplied working gives 2a + b = −16 and −a + b = −10, then a = −2, b = −12.
entries.exclusionReason: Worked example is reference evidence only.

entries.description: How do we find the remainder when the divisor is quadratic? Use P(x) = D(x)Q(x) + R(x); R(x) should be linear at most.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone explanation is reference evidence only.

entries.description: example — Remainder of quadratic divisor. Let P(x) = x⁹⁹ − 1. Find the remainder on division by (x − 1)(x + 1). Supplied identity uses remainder Ax + B, annotated deg R(x) < 2. Substitution gives 0 = A + B and −2 = −A + B; A = 1, B = −1; remainder x − 1.
entries.exclusionReason: Worked example and meaningful degree annotation are reference evidence only.

entries.description: example — Unknown P(x). P(x) has remainder 2 on division by x + 1 and remainder −1 on division by x − 2. Find the remainder on division by x² − x − 2. Supplied identity factors the divisor as (x − 2)(x + 1), with remainder Ax + B. P(−1) = 2 = −A + B and P(2) = −1 = 2A + B; A = −1, B = 1; remainder −x + 1.
entries.exclusionReason: Worked example and factorisation annotation are reference evidence only.

entries.description: Roots and zeroes; definition — Roots and zeroes. Values α satisfying P(α) = 0 are zeroes; solutions of aₙxⁿ + aₙ₋₁xⁿ⁻¹ + ⋯ + a₁x + a₀ = 0 are roots. Illustrations use (x − 1)(x − 2) and values 1, 2.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone definitions and illustrative statements are teaching reference evidence only.

entries.description: reminder: Roots and zeroes are often used interchangeably; roots refer to solutions of polynomial equations and zeroes to inputs yielding zero.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone reminder is teaching reference evidence only.

entries.description: Factor theorem; theorem — Factor theorem. If P(α) = 0 then x − α is a factor. Proof invokes the remainder theorem.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone theorem, proof and explanatory transition are teaching reference evidence only.

entries.description: theorem — Integer root theorem. For a polynomial equation with integer coefficients, an integer root α must divide the constant term a₀. Supplied proof rearranges the polynomial equation to α times a combination of integers = −a₀.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone theorem and proof are teaching reference evidence only.

entries.description: example — Using the integer root theorem to factorise a polynomial. Express P(x) = 2x³ − 9x² + 7x + 6 as a product of polynomials with integer coefficients. Test factors of 6: P(1) = 6, P(−1) = −12, P(2) = 0. Divide by x − 2 using supplied long division; quotient 2x² − 5x − 3. Final supplied factorisation: (x − 2)(x − 3)(2x + 1). Margin cue: Find one factor and divide.
entries.exclusionReason: Worked example, long-division scaffold and method cue are teaching reference evidence only.

entries.description: note to students: A method that avoids long division is shown in the appendix.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone note is reference evidence only; the appendix method is not supplied here.

entries.description: What if none of the factors worked? Failure of integer-root candidates establishes no integer roots, but rational roots may remain. For a reduced rational root p/q, p divides a₀ and q divides aₙ.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone explanation and rational-root conditions are teaching reference evidence only.

entries.description: Rational-root illustration: possible rational roots of 6x³ + 5x² − 3x − 2 = 0 are ±1, ±2, ±1/2, ±1/3, ±2/3, ±1/6, obtained from factors of 2 divided by factors of 6. Printed continuation: If none of them work, the roots must be irrational.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone teaching illustration is reference evidence only.

entries.description: example — Using factors of the leading coefficient. Express P(x) = 12x³ + 8x² − 13x + 3 as a product of polynomials with integer coefficients. Supplied tests: P(1) = 10, P(−1) = 12, P(3) = 360, P(−3) = −210. Then test factors of 3 divided by factors of 12: P(1/2) = 0, so 2x − 1 is a factor. Further supplied zeroes −3/2 and 1/3 give (2x − 1)(2x + 3)(3x − 1); long division is also offered.
entries.exclusionReason: Worked example is teaching reference evidence only.

entries.description: Using x − b/a or ax − b. The preceding factorisation (2x − 1)(2x + 3)(3x − 1) can be written 12(x − 1/2)(x + 3/2)(x − 1/3) by extracting each coefficient of x.

entries.description: Context PDF page 9, printed page 109: 2B Remainder and factor theorem; Remainder theorem; theorem subtitle Remainder Theorem. Given a polynomial P(x), division by x − a leaves remainder P(a). Proof uses P(x) = (x − a)Q(x) + R and substitutes x = a.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone theorem and proof; reference teaching evidence only.

entries.description: Context PDF page 9: note to students — This allows you to skip the division algorithm when finding the remainder.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone teaching note; not selectable practice.

entries.description: Context PDF page 9: example — Remainder of linear divisor. Find the remainder when P(x) = x^99 − 1 is divided by x + 1. Supplied solution: R = P(−1) = (−1)^99 − 1 = −2.
entries.exclusionReason: Worked example; reference evidence only.

entries.description: Context PDF page 9: example — Finding polynomials with given remainder. P(x) = x^3 + 3x^2 + ax + b has remainder 4 on division by x − 2 and remainder −8 on division by x + 1. Find a and b. Supplied solution forms 2a + b = −16 and −a + b = −10, then obtains a = −2, b = −12.
entries.exclusionReason: Worked example; reference evidence only.

entries.description: Context PDF page 9: How do we find the remainder when the divisor is quadratic? Express P(x) = D(x)Q(x) + R(x); the remainder R(x) should be linear at most.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone explanatory teaching region.

entries.description: Context PDF page 10, printed page 110: example — Remainder of quadratic divisor. Let P(x) = x^99 − 1. Find the remainder on division by (x − 1)(x + 1). Supplied solution writes x^99 − 1 = (x − 1)(x + 1)Q(x) + Ax + B, annotates deg R(x) < 2, substitutes x = 1 and −1, obtains A = 1, B = −1, and remainder x − 1.
entries.exclusionReason: Worked example, including its meaningful degree annotation; reference only, not a new practice diagram.

entries.description: Context PDF page 10: example — Unknown P(x). P(x) has remainder 2 on division by x + 1 and remainder −1 on division by x − 2. Find the remainder on division by x^2 − x − 2. Supplied solution factorises the divisor as (x − 2)(x + 1), writes a remainder Ax + B, forms −A + B = 2 and 2A + B = −1, obtains A = −1, B = 1, and remainder −x + 1.
entries.exclusionReason: Worked example, including divisor-factorisation annotation; reference only.

entries.description: Context PDF page 11, printed page 111: Roots and zeroes; definition — Roots and zeroes. Values α with P(α) = 0 are zeroes of the polynomial function. Solutions of a_n x^n + a_(n−1)x^(n−1) + ⋯ + a_1x + a_0 = 0 are roots of the polynomial equation.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone definition; reference only.

entries.description: Context PDF page 11: reminder — roots and zeroes often name the same values; roots refer to solutions of equations and zeroes to inputs yielding zero.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone reminder; reference only.

entries.description: Context PDF page 11: (x − 1)(x − 2) = 0 has roots x = 1, 2; P(x) = (x − 1)(x − 2) has zeroes x = 1, 2.
entries.exclusionReason: Supplied explanatory illustration, not a practice task.

entries.description: Context PDF page 11: Factor theorem; theorem — Factor theorem. If P(α) = 0, then x − α is a factor. Proof applies the remainder theorem.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone theorem and proof; reference only.

entries.description: Context PDF page 11: theorem — Integer root theorem. For a polynomial equation with integer coefficients, any integer root α is a factor of the constant term a_0. Proof rearranges the root identity to α times an integer = −a_0.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone theorem and proof, including the meaningful integer-combination annotation; reference only.

entries.description: Context PDF page 12, printed page 112: example — Using the integer root theorem to factorise a polynomial. Express P(x) = 2x^3 − 9x^2 + 7x + 6 as a product of polynomials with integer coefficients. Supplied solution tests P(1) = 6, P(−1) = −12, P(2) = 0, divides by x − 2 using full long division, obtains quotient 2x^2 − 5x − 3, and factorises as (x − 2)(x − 3)(2x + 1).
entries.exclusionReason: Worked example and supplied long-division scaffold; reference only.

entries.description: Context PDF page 12: note to students — A method that avoids long division is shown in the appendix.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone reference note; appendix method is not supplied or required for this inventory.

entries.description: Context PDF page 12: What if none of the factors worked? Failed integer-root candidates do not exclude rational roots. Rational root theorem: for a root p/q in simplest terms, p divides a_0 and q divides a_n.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone explanatory teaching region.

entries.description: Context PDF page 13, printed page 113: possible rational roots of 6x^3 + 5x^2 − 3x − 2 = 0 are ±1, ±2, ±1/2, ±1/3, ±2/3, ±1/6. Printed concluding sentence: If none of them work, the roots must be irrational.

entries.description: Let H(x) = P(x) − x. The given conditions become H(x) ≥ 0, H(1) = 0, H(2) = 1, H(3) = 0. A graph of y = H(x) fulfilling these conditions shows that it must have equation H(x) = k(x − 1)^2(x − 3)^2 and H(2) = 1, which gives k = 1. So, H(4) = (4 − 1)^2(4 − 3)^2 = 9. Since H(4) = P(4) − 4, then 9 = P(4) − 4, so P(4) = 13.

entries.description: Introduction to polynomials. A polynomial has the form a_n x^n + a_(n−1)x^(n−1) + ⋯ + a_1x + a_0. Polynomials can be added, subtracted and multiplied together to form another polynomial. The division transformation identity states that any polynomial P(x) can be expressed in the form D(x)Q(x) + R(x), where deg(R(x)) < deg(D(x)). Apply the division algorithm to find quotient and remainders in polynomial division.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone summary material on context PDF page 48, printed page 148; reference evidence only.

entries.description: Remainder and factor theorem. If a polynomial is divided by x − a, the remainder is equal to P(a). When the divisor is not linear, use the division transformation identity. If P(a) = 0 then x − a is a factor.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone summary material on context PDF page 48, printed page 148; reference evidence only.

entries.description: Graphs of polynomial functions. α is a root/zero of multiplicity m when P(x) = (x − α)^m Q(x) and x − α is not a factor of Q(x). The leading term determines the behaviour of P(x) as x → ±∞. As x → ∞: if n is even and a_n > 0, then P(x) → ∞; if n is even and a_n < 0, then P(x) → −∞; if n is odd and a_n > 0, then P(x) → −∞; if n is odd and a_n < 0, then P(x) → ∞. Zeroes correspond to x-intercepts on the graph of y = P(x). Repeated zeroes of multiplicity m look like simple degree m curves near the x-intercept.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone summary material on context PDF page 48, printed page 148; reference evidence only.

resolution.reason: Preserve the original reference pixels.
